awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I: Flexible Sensor Arrays for Smart Fabrics and Surfaces using Ink-jet Printing and a Practical Approach to Nanotechnology
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project seeks to advance the practicality of smart materials and the Internet-of-Things (IoT) by featuring a low-profile carbon nanotube (CNT) sensor that can detect low-force impacts, micro-sized bending strains, damage features in materials, and human finger movements.  Organisms understand their environment by experiencing and learning from experienced sensations. From a technological perspective, at the core of intelligence, sensory organs collect signals and transduce them into computable information. The project goal is to instill this process of feeling into inanimate objects. Integrating CNT sensors into materials will enable smart surfaces, health monitoring of structures and machinery, haptic feedback systems, and human-machine interfaces.  The scalability and affordability of these sensor components will bolster the commercial appeal of devices across all of these applications areas. For perspective, the global Internet-of-Things sensor market size is currently valued at $16 billion, and this is expected to grow to $70 billion over the next five years. This project will focus on scaling individual devices into sensing arrays that transduce mechanical stress into valuable sensory data. 

The intellectual merit of this project is based on the creation of valuable technical data and the ability to demonstrate a novel application of cutting-edge nanotechnology. The sensors to be developed rely on carbon nanotube buckypaper (CNT-BP) and its inherent ability to detect stress and strain better than many commercial sensors. The combination of effectiveness and efficiency displayed by these devices hold promise for commercial adoption. This project aims to explore the advantages and limitations of CNT-BP sensors in various situations. Though CNT-based sensors have been studied throughout the years, this project will introduce a patented process for scalable production. To prove the practicality of the technology, the overarching project goals include measuring the reliability of the featured sensor, scaling the sensors into arrays for spatial recognition, and enabling human-machine interfacing via wearable sensor integrations. The technical objectives include the collection of reliability metrics (sensitivity, resolution, stretchability, and durability), the mapping of stress and strain throughout relevant materials, and the translation of biometric data into relevant signals for the chosen use cases.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Aging bridges and commercial buildings accumulate unseen internal stress between periodic visual walkthroughs, hiding progressive material damage until costly or catastrophic failures occur. Existing structural health monitoring (SHM) hardware remains too expensive and complex for widespread deployment, leaving building stewards, licensed engineers, and transportation agencies without real-time visibility. 
To solve this problem, FWM completed an STTR Phase I project validating the reliability, manufacturing scalability, and commercial feasibility of patented carbon nanotube Buckypaper (CNT-BP) thin-film strain sensors. Fabricated through a lean, emission-free workflow combining scalable CNT-BP filtration with commercial inkjet-printed silver circuitry on flexible polymer substrates, these <0.02 mm sensors operate passively below 1 volt without external amplifiers and cost under $1 per node in raw materials.
Building on this scalable manufacturing process, FWM produced more than 100 standardized sensors and established a baseline technical data sheet quantifying sensitivity, mechanical limits, and cyclic endurance. Under standardized three-point flexural bending on composite coupons, the sensors achieved an empirical gauge factor exceeding 400, which is more than 200 times higher than conventional metallic foil strain gauges, and detected structural deflections below 1 millimeter. Tensile evaluations confirmed an average ultimate strain tolerance of 13.5% before failure, while dynamic fatigue testing verified continuous operation past 19,200 cycles, outlasting a 3D-printed host coupon to record structural fracture with distinct electrical spikes.
Scaling from laboratory coupons to full-scale testbeds, FWM integrated the sensors into diverse SHM and wearable scenarios. Across rigid composite panels, multi-sensor arrays localized low-force impacts and distinguished pristine structures from internally damaged panels. On 2-foot composite I-beams under hydraulic bending, discrete sensor nodes mapped flexural strain gradients and localized failure modes alongside a $100,000+ optical Digital Image Correlation system, while rough-in embedment trials confirmed that bare sensors survive inside wet-cast mineral cylinders without weakening the host structure. Exploring additional sensor applications beyond civil infrastructure, the team also integrated sensor nodes onto a biometric glove with onboard baseline-conditioning firmware to wirelessly actuate a robotic hand.
